Field surveys of the Halfbanded rockfish (Sebastes semicinctus) indicate that this viviparous species produces offspring that are exceptionally small upon parturition. The mass of a newly released larva is approximately 0.000268 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000268 grams], a value consistent with the minute egg diameter of about 0.8 millimeters observed in gravid females. This remarkably low natal mass is characteristic of many rockfishes that produce large numbers of pelagic larvae, a strategy that offsets high early-life mortality through sheer numerical output. The tiny size of these larvae necessitates a prolonged period in the plankton, during which they feed on copepod nauplii and other microzooplankton before transitioning to a demersal existence, a phase that requires substantial somatic growth before the onset of gonadal maturation.

As individuals grow, they eventually reach a total length indicative of reproductive maturation. Puberty is attained when females measure approximately 11 centimeters [Lp = approximately 11 centimeters] in total length, a size that typically corresponds to the second or third year of life in southern California populations. At this developmental milestone, a female achieves a wet weight of about 9 grams [Wwp = about 9 grams], reflecting the necessary energetic reserves required to support vitellogenesis and the ensuing gestation period. This size at maturity is relatively modest compared to congeners like the cowcod (Sebastes levis), which delay maturation until much larger body sizes, suggesting that Halfbanded rockfish adopt a more rapid life-history schedule potentially linked to higher natural mortality rates in their preferred rocky-reef and kelp-forest habitats.

The ultimate body size for this species is defined by a maximum recorded total length of 25 centimeters [Li = 25 centimeters]. Based on a length-weight relationship typical for the genus, this length corresponds to an asymptotic wet body mass of 105.6 grams [Wwi = 105.6 grams], a moderate adult size that places it among the smaller members of the subgenus Sebastomus. This ultimate size is attained through several years of steady growth, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of sexual maturity as energy is increasingly directed toward reproduction rather than somatic development. The relationship between length and mass in this species follows a cubic power law, conforming to the general isometric growth pattern observed across many marine teleosts, though individual variation in body condition can fluctuate seasonally with prey availability.

Reproductive investment in Halfbanded rockfish is substantial, with females capable of producing multiple broods during a single spawning season. Under the prevailing thermal conditions of their environment, typically 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C], the maximum annual reproductive output is considerable; each female releases several thousand larvae per brood [N_R_i = several thousand larvae per brood] and can complete approximately 3 to 4 broods per season [F_R_i = approximately 3 to 4 broods per season], a rate sustained over the extended parturition period. This fecundity offsets the severe mortality pressures faced by the pelagic larvae, which are vulnerable to predation by zooplanktivorous fishes and chaetognaths throughout their protracted larval drift.

Longevity data for Sebastes semicinctus indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 15 years [am = approximately 15 years] when reared at 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C], a duration that is intermediate among eastern Pacific rockfishes. This species exhibits a classic iteroparous life cycle, with individuals spawning repeatedly over several seasons rather than perishing after a single reproductive event. The oldest documented individuals have been recorded at an age of roughly 5475 days [am = roughly 5475 days] in waters averaging 9.2 °C, demonstrating the capacity for extended reproductive output that buffers populations against variable recruitment at a temperature of 9.2 °C [T = 9.2 °C] success. Such longevity is ecologically significant because it allows multiple overlapping generations within a given habitat, promoting population stability despite the stochastic nature of larval survival in the dynamic California Current ecosystem.
